title: Absolute liability — M.C. Mehta (Oleum Gas Leak)

content.overview: Absolute liability, formulated in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak), holds that an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity owes an absolute and non-delegable duty to the community. Escape of a hazardous substance attracting this rule does not admit the Rylands exceptions. Compensation is correlated to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Justice P.N. Bhagwati's formulation responds to industrial risk in Indian conditions. Where the activity is hazardous or inherently dangerous, the enterprise must absorb the cost of harm from that activity. The duty is non-delegable.

sections.heading: No Rylands exceptions
sections.body: Act of God, stranger, and related Rylands exceptions do not dilute absolute liability once the rule applies. That is the doctrinal break from strict liability.

sections.heading: Measure of compensation
sections.body: Compensation should reflect the enterprise's magnitude and capacity — a deterrent and restorative measure suited to large hazardous industries, not a purely nominal figure.

sections.heading: Track B
sections.body: Frame pleadings around hazardous activity, control by the enterprise, escape/harm, and community injury. Cite M.C. Mehta for the rule; do not invent paragraph numbers. Parallel public-law remedies under Articles 32/226 may coexist in appropriate facts (constitutional tort / public law compensation).

enhancement.definition: Absolute liability is the Indian rule that an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity has an absolute and non-delegable duty to ensure that no harm results from that activity.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: For hazardous industries, the Supreme Court developed a stricter rule than Rylands v Fletcher, without the traditional exceptions.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Indian tort law is largely uncodified. The governing rules are developed through common-law principles, Indian judicial decisions and applicable legislation for particular fields. Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 (Act 6 of 1991), Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II, Section 1, No. 8, 23 January 1991, opened at https://moef.gov.in/uploads/pdf-uploads/pdf_693024ea7c3633.90180378.pdf. Section 3(1) makes the owner liable to give Schedule relief where death or injury to a person other than a workman, or property damage, results from an accident. Section 3(2) is no-fault: the claimant need not plead or establish wrongful act, neglect or default. Section 4 requires insurance against section 3 relief before handling a hazardous substance, with a one-year transition and a notified exemption only if a fund is maintained. Section 8(1) says the right to section 3 relief is in addition to any other right to claim compensation; section 8(2) reduces that other compensation by relief paid under the Act. The 1991 Schedule figures (Rs 25,000 fatal relief, Rs 12,500 medical cap, Rs 25,000 total permanent disability, wage relief not exceeding Rs 1,000 a month for up to 3 months, property damage up to Rs 6,000) are the Gazette figures only. Later amendment amounts and the commencement notification were not opened, so current figures are not certified. Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023 (18 of 2023), Gazette Extraordinary No. 21, 11 August 2023, serial 28, opened. G.S.R. 756(E), 18 October 2023, appoints 1 April 2024 as the date those Public Liability Insurance Act entries come into force. From that date section 3(1) is substituted: the owner is liable to reimburse such amount, or provide such other relief as may be prescribed, for death, medical expenses, loss of wages, other injury or sickness, damage to private property, or other prescribed loss. The 1991 Schedule figures are therefore not the current statutory measure. The rules prescribing the post-1 April 2024 amounts were not opened, so no current rupee figure is certified. Public Liability Insurance (Amendment) Rules, 2024, G.S.R. 772(E), 17 December 2024, opened at https://moef.gov.in/storage/tender/1735217194.pdf. Rule 10(5) says the owner shall reimburse or provide relief under section 3(1) as specified in the Schedule to those rules. The Second Schedule states: fatal-accident relief Rs 5,00,000 per person plus medical expenses up to Rs 1,50,000; permanent total disability cash relief Rs 5,00,000 plus medical expenses up to Rs 25,000; temporary partial disability wage relief actual amount not exceeding Rs 25,000 per month for up to 3 months if hospitalised more than 3 days and above 16; private-property damage not exceeding Rs 50,00,000 depending on actual damage; other injury or sickness reimbursement not exceeding Rs 25,000. Rule 10(1) caps the insurance-policy aggregate at Rs 250 crore, and Rs 500 crore for more than one accident during the policy or one year, whichever is less. These are the prescribed amounts opened. They do not replace the M.C. Mehta measure of compensation.

caseLaw.name: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak case)
caseLaw.holding: Judgment dated 20/12/1986. An enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity owes an absolute and non-delegable duty. If harm results from an accident in that activity, for example escape of toxic gas, the enterprise is strictly and absolutely liable to compensate those affected, and that liability is not subject to the exceptions which operate under Rylands v. Fletcher. Compensation must be correlated to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise. The Court did not decide whether Shriram was 'State' under Article 12, and directed the Delhi Legal Aid and Advice Board to file compensation actions rather than awarding compensation in that order.
caseLaw.relevance: Direct authority for the Indian absolute-liability formulation used in this topic.
